Learning Objective (LO) 1 · Integrated gastrointestinal/genitourinary (GI/GU) historyRubric · Communication
Start with the story

History, localization & abdominal landmarks

LECTURE pp. 8–15 · transcript history discussion

The abdominal exam is most useful when the history has already narrowed the field. Build the complaint with Location, Onset, Provocation/Palliation, Quality, Radiation, Severity, Timing, and Associated symptoms (LOPQRSTA), then ask targeted GI/GU symptoms and use the location to ask a simple question: what lives there?

LOPQRSTA for abdominal pain

  • Location — quadrant/region; focal vs diffuse.
  • Onset — sudden suggests an acute process; chronic suggests a chronic disease pattern.
  • Provocation / Palliation — meals, movement, position, defecation.
  • Quality — burning, colicky, sharp, pressure, gnawing.
  • Radiation — mid-epigastric → back can point toward pancreas; right upper quadrant (RUQ) → right shoulder/scapula can point toward biliary/liver disease.
  • Severity / Timing — episodic vs progressive vs constant.
  • Associated symptoms — fever, nausea/vomiting (N/V), bowel or urinary change, jaundice, bleeding.

review of systems (ROS) that matters

General: fever, chills, weakness, night sweats, weight change, sleep change, fatigue.

GI: abdominal pain, N/V, diarrhea, constipation, heartburn, dysphagia, gas, bilious/bloody emesis, hematochezia, melena, pale stool, prior endoscopy/colonoscopy.

GU: dysuria, hematuria, frequency, leakage, incomplete emptying, change in stream, flank/back/groin pain.

Context: medications (especially nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for gastritis/ulcer clues), family history, prior surgery.

🧠 Memory hook
“What lives there + what travels from there?” Location localizes the organ; radiation often tells you the direction of referred pain.
AreaStructures emphasized in the courseClinical thought
RUQLiver, gallbladder, some pancreas/bowel, partial right kidney/adrenalBiliary/liver disease; consider renal source if flank/costovertebral angle (CVA) features.
left upper quadrant (LUQ)Stomach, spleen, some liver/pancreas/bowel, partial left kidney/adrenalGastric, splenic, pancreatic, renal patterns.

Check yourself 1
A patient reports mid-epigastric pain that “goes straight through” to the back. Which radiation pattern should immediately enter your differential?
Pancreatic pain. Mid-epigastric pain radiating to the back is a pancreatic clue.
Learning Objective (LO) 1 · Physical examRubric · Part 1
The order matters

Inspection → Auscultation → Percussion → Palpation

LECTURE pp. 15–21 · RUBRIC pp. 5–6
Exam sequence
I → A → P → P: Inspect, Auscultate, Percuss, Palpate. Auscultation comes before percussion/palpation.

1 · Inspect

Contour, abdominal wall movement, skin lesions/color, bruising, scars, distention, hernias/bulges, masses, visible aortic pulsation.

2 · Auscultate

Bowel sounds in at least one area, then listen over aorta + bilateral renal + bilateral iliac arteries. Rubric skips femorals.

3 · Percuss

Four quadrants + epigastric + suprapubic regions, then liver and spleen. Distinguish tympany (air) from dullness (solid/fluid/feces).

4 · Palpate

Light then deep in all six areas. Look for tenderness, masses, voluntary vs involuntary guarding. Palpate liver and spleen.

Patient setup + safety

  • Usually supine; arms at sides so the abdominal wall relaxes.
  • Pillow under head; knees may be flexed for comfort/relaxation.
  • Obtain consent and explicitly allow the patient to stop at any time.
  • Drape appropriately and re-consent if moving the drape.
  • Examine the painful area last.
  • Watch the face/body for discomfort even when the patient does not verbalize it.

Normal vs abnormal anchors

  • Normal bowel sounds: 5–34/min; <5 hypoactive, >34 hyperactive.
  • Bruits = turbulent “whooshing” arterial flow; a bruit with a pulsatile mass raises concern for vascular disease/abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA).
  • Friction rub = rare grating sound; can accompany peritoneal or organ-surface pathology.
  • Typical abdomen is mostly tympanitic; liver is dull.
  • Involuntary guarding persists despite relaxation maneuvers and is more concerning for peritoneal irritation.
Patient-friendly language
“I’m going to listen to your stomach sounds and the blood flow in your abdomen.”
“I’ll press in several areas. Please tell me if anything is tender or if you want me to stop.”

Second year: keep the medical terminology in your head; speak to the patient in plain language.

Check yourself 2
You have already inspected the abdomen. What should you do next: percuss, palpate, or auscultate?
Auscultate. The course sequence is I-A-P-P.
Learning Objective (LO) 3 · Liver/spleen/kidneysRubric · Organ exam
Technique is context-dependent

Liver, spleen, kidneys & aorta

LECTURE pp. 19–23 · transcript technique comparison

There is more than one acceptable way to examine these organs. The technique should match the patient, setting, complaint, and your index of suspicion — especially when organ enlargement is possible.

Liver percussion

  1. Right midclavicular line.
  2. Start near nipple level and percuss down to dullness = superior border.
  3. Start in right lower quadrant (RLQ) and percuss upward to dullness = inferior border.

Expected span: 6–12 cm at midclavicular line (MCL). A single top-to-bottom percussion sequence is also used by some clinicians.

Liver palpation

Normal edge, if felt, is soft, smooth, distinct. It may descend with inspiration and can be palpable up to about 3 cm below the right costal margin without implying hepatomegaly.

If hepatomegaly is suspected, start low (even RLQ) and move upward so you do not miss a markedly enlarged edge. Hooking under the costal margin can work when the liver is normal/mildly enlarged.

Spleen

Enlargement proceeds anteriorly, downward, and medially. Two percussion options:

  • Traube space: expected tympany; dullness suggests enlargement.
  • Castell sign: lowest left anterior axillary interspace stays tympanitic with inspiration; new dullness suggests splenomegaly.

About 5% of normal patients may have a palpable splenic tip.

Kidney bimanual palpation

Supine. Place one hand posteriorly between the lower rib cage and iliac crest and the other anteriorly below the costal margin. Press the hands toward each other while the patient takes a deep breath; try to capture the lower pole.

Kidneys can be difficult to palpate; enlargement such as polycystic kidney disease may make them easier to appreciate.

Aorta

Feel pulsations by pressing deeply just left of the abdominal midline in the epigastric area. Then estimate width with hands on both sides.

Rubric normal: ≤3 cm wide. A pulsatile mass ± bruit is concerning for abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA).

Same organ, different question

OrganTechniqueWhat it tells youWhen it is especially useful
LiverPercussion of spanEstimates superior/inferior borders and overall span.Screening for enlargement; useful even when edge is not palpable.
LiverLow-to-high palpation / hookingEdge position, texture, smoothness, tenderness.Start lower when hepatomegaly is suspected; hooking is more practical around the costal margin when enlargement is not marked.
SpleenTraube-space percussionLoss of expected tympany may suggest enlargement.Quick screen for splenomegaly.
SpleenCastell inspiratory percussionNew dullness with deep inspiration suggests enlargement.Alternative percussion maneuver when a more focused inspiratory test is desired.
SpleenPalpationAttempts to feel the descending splenic tip.More convincing when positive; a negative exam does not exclude splenomegaly.
KidneyBimanual palpationSize/fullness and ability to capture the lower pole.When enlargement or a renal mass is suspected.
Kidneycostovertebral angle (CVA) percussionElicits pain rather than size.Flank pain, pyelonephritis, stone, or renal irritation.
Evidence-based reality check

Liver percussion ≥10 cm MCL: sensitivity 61–92%, specificity 30–43%. Palpable spleen for splenomegaly: sensitivity 17–78%, specificity 89–99%, positive likelihood ratio (LR+) 8.4. A negative maneuver can miss disease; a convincingly palpable spleen is more useful for ruling in enlargement than ruling it out.

Check yourself 3
Why can starting liver palpation only at the right costal margin be a problem when hepatomegaly is strongly suspected?
A markedly enlarged liver edge may be well below the costal margin, so a low-to-high search helps avoid missing it.

Choose ≥3 based on symptoms

Special tests: technique → positive finding → meaning

🧠 Appendicitis cluster
R-M-P-O: Rovsing, McBurney, Psoas, Obturator. Rebound and heel strike add evidence of peritoneal irritation.

CVA anatomy

The costovertebral angle is formed by the 12th rib and upper lumbar vertebral region. Tenderness localizes the differential toward the kidney/upper urinary tract.

Fluid falls; dullness follows.
Check yourself 4
A tender spot hurts just as much after the patient lifts the head and tenses the abdominal muscles. What does that suggest?
A positive Carnett sign: the pain is more likely arising from the abdominal wall rather than a deeper intra-abdominal source.
Learning Objective (LO) 5 · Chronic liver diseaseLO 6 · Ominous abdominal signs
Pattern recognition by inspection

Chronic liver disease, caput medusae, Grey Turner, Cullen & Sister Mary Joseph

LECTURE pp. 29–32

Skin / vascular

  • Spider angiomas
  • Palmar erythema
  • Jaundice
  • Scleral icterus
  • Caput medusae

Endocrine / systemic

  • Gynecomastia
  • Testicular atrophy
  • Hair loss
  • Clubbing

Other clues

  • Parotid enlargement — particularly with alcohol-related disease; may reflect alcohol more than the liver itself.
  • Dupuytren contracture

No single item is specific; the constellation matters.

Venous flow diagram · caput medusae
Portal hypertension
→
portal blood seeks collateral route
→
periumbilical / umbilical veins open
→
blood enters superficial abdominal wall veins
→
prominent radiating veins
caput medusae

Grey Turner sign

Ecchymotic discoloration along the flank. The lecture image is in the setting of acute pancreatitis and notes retroperitoneal blood tracking into subcutaneous tissue.

Cullen sign

Periumbilical bruising/ecchymosis. Recognize the location: Grey = flank; Cullen = umbilicus.

Sister Mary Joseph nodule

Firm dermal/subcutaneous umbilical nodule from metastatic carcinoma, most often adenocarcinoma. Sources listed: stomach, large bowel, ovary, pancreas. An ominous finding.

🧠 Image hook
Grey goes to the sides; Cullen circles the center. Sister Mary Joseph sits at the umbilicus as a metastatic nodule, not a bruise.
Check yourself 5
A vignette describes a firm umbilical subcutaneous nodule in a patient with weight loss. Which named finding is this?
Sister Mary Joseph nodule — an umbilical metastasis, often from an adenocarcinoma.

Pattern → test → plan

The abdominal pain matrix: discriminate the 11 named processes

OBJECTIVE COMPLETION · deck directs these details to Bates Table 21-2
Source boundary — one time only
The uploaded slides name these 11 disease processes but refer you to Bates Tables 21-2/21-4 for the detailed symptom matrix; those textbook rows are not included in the uploaded files. The table below is a concise standard clinical synthesis so the stated objective is usable. Rubric maneuvers, numeric cutoffs, screening recommendations, diet details, and the acute-abdomen case work-up elsewhere on this page mirror the uploaded course materials.
ProcessLocation / quality / timingAggravating / alleviatingAssociated cluesBest next diagnostic anchorInitial treatment / disposition anchor
gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)Retrosternal or epigastric burning; recurrentWorse after meals, recumbency, bending; often better with acid suppressionSour regurgitation, cough/hoarseness; alarm = dysphagia, bleeding, weight lossClassic uncomplicated symptoms often clinical/proton pump inhibitor (PPI) trial; esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) for alarm features or refractory disease.Lifestyle trigger control + acid suppression (often PPI); escalate evaluation for alarm/refractory features.

Gastric cancerPersistent epigastric discomfort, progressiveMay worsen with eating as disease advancesEarly satiety, anorexia, weight loss, iron-deficiency anemia, occult bleedingEGD with biopsy; staging imaging after tissue diagnosis.Multidisciplinary staging; resection when feasible ± systemic therapy depending on stage.
AppendicitisClassically vague periumbilical pain → right lower quadrant (RLQ); becomes focal/steadyMovement worsens painAnorexia, nausea/vomiting (N/V), fever; McBurney/Rovsing/Psoas/Obturator; guarding/reboundCBC, urinalysis (UA), pregnancy test when relevant; computed tomography (CT) with intravenous (IV) contrast in many adults; ultrasound (US) / magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in selected patients.Surgical evaluation; antibiotics and appendectomy are common definitive pathways, tailored to complication/risk.

Acute diverticulitisUsually left lower quadrant (LLQ) steady painOften worsens over hours-daysFever, bowel habit change, focal tendernessCT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast when imaging is needed; CBC.Uncomplicated disease may be managed supportively/selectively with antibiotics; admit/drain/operate for selected complicated disease.

🧠 Fast discrimination
Burning → acid (gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) / peptic ulcer disease (PUD)). RUQ + Murphy → cholecystitis. Epigastric → back → pancreas. Periumbilical → RLQ → appendicitis. LLQ + fever → diverticulitis. Colicky + distention + obstipation → obstruction. Pain ≫ exam → mesenteric ischemia.

Acute abdominal pain: course work-up anchors

Initial labs from the lab case

  • CBC
  • CMP
  • Urinalysis
  • Urine human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) when pregnancy is possible

Pregnancy changes the imaging/differential algorithm.

Imaging logic emphasized

  • RUQ → ultrasound is the first localization study for suspected cholecystitis.
  • Lower abdominal/reproductive differential → pelvic exam and often pelvic US; MRI can be considered.
  • CT with contrast is common for acute abdominal pain; the lab notes IV contrast is typical and oral contrast is generally not used in the acute setting.
  • Mesenteric ischemia risk → CT angiography.

Assessment

State the single most likely diagnosis and the specific history/exam facts that support it.

Differential

Defend alternatives using VINDICATES, systems, or “what lives here”; explicitly say what supports and what argues against each.

Plan

Choose tests that answer the uncertainty, then treatment/disposition that matches severity. In an unstable or peritoneal patient, do not keep performing low-value painful maneuvers.

Check yourself 6
A patient has sudden severe abdominal pain that seems dramatically worse than the early abdominal exam. Which process must stay high on the list, and what imaging test is the key diagnostic anchor?
Mesenteric ischemia → CT angiography. “Pain out of proportion” is the classic discrimination clue.

Learning Objective (LO) 11 · Celiac disease
Diet is the treatment

Celiac disease: gluten-free diet & follow-up

LAB pp. 16–25

The lab case moves from chronic diarrhea and iron deficiency to positive tissue transglutaminase immunoglobulin A (tTG-IgA) and esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) biopsy consistent with celiac disease, then focuses on counseling and monitoring.

Avoid

Wheat · rye · barley

  • Read labels: gluten can appear in stabilizers/additives.
  • Beer, ale, lager and malt vinegar commonly use gluten-containing grain.
  • Initially avoid oats; they may be reintroduced once controlled with close monitoring because contamination is a concern.

Safe alternatives listed

Soybean/tapioca flours, rice, corn, buckwheat, potatoes.

Some patients also have lactose intolerance.

🧠 Memory hook
WRB = Wrong for the Bowel: Wheat, Rye, Barley.

At diagnosis

Check nutritional deficiencies: vitamins A, D, E, B12, folate, ferritin/iron, prothrombin time. If clinically indicated, consider thiamine, B6, magnesium, copper, zinc, selenium.

3–6 months

Clinical follow-up after starting the diet; check complete blood count (CBC), folate, B12, iron, liver chemistries, and celiac serology.

Long term

Annual hemoglobin, iron, folate and serologic monitoring. tTG-IgA or IgA deamidated gliadin peptide (DGP) at 6–12 months after diagnosis, then annually.

Do not overinterpret a normalized tTG
Normal IgA tTG does not reliably prove villous healing. There is also substantial inter-assay variation; use the same laboratory when possible for longitudinal comparison.

Diet recommendation nuance from the lab

A gluten-free diet is recommended for serologically + histologically confirmed celiac disease and for symptomatic potential celiac disease. The lab notes it is not routinely recommended for latent/asymptomatic potential disease with normal small-bowel biopsy; monitor and re-biopsy as indicated because disease can be patchy.

Check yourself 8
A celiac patient’s tTG-IgA normalizes after dietary treatment. Can you conclude that the villi have healed?
No. The lab explicitly warns that normalized IgA tTG does not reliably indicate improved villous architecture.
Learning Objective (LO) 12 · irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) diet
Start simple, escalate thoughtfully

Irritable bowel syndrome: basic diet vs low-fermentable oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides, and polyols (FODMAP)

LAB pp. 26–31

IBS framing

Chronic disorder of brain–gut interaction with abdominal pain and altered bowel habits without another explanatory pathology.

Rome intravenous (IV) as presented: recurrent abdominal pain at least once/week for the last 3 months, associated with ≥2 of: related to defecation, change in stool frequency, change in stool form. Then determine subtype.

Treatment frame

  • Support the diagnosis and validate symptoms.
  • Set realistic expectations and arrange follow-up.
  • Behavior: physical activity + sleep.
  • Diet: traditional IBS diet and/or FODMAP.
  • Adjunct pharmacotherapy based on subtype.
  • Experiment and individualize.
Traditional IBS diet firstLow-FODMAP if needed / motivated
Eat at regular mealtimes; avoid long gaps; smaller, more frequent meals.Eliminate high-FODMAP foods for 4–6 weeks.
Limit gas-producing foods, high-fat/fried foods, lactose-containing foods, insoluble fiber, and personal triggers.Assess clinical response.
Increase soluble fiber: psyllium/ispaghula, oat bran, barley, legumes.If improved, slowly reintroduce one food every 3 days to identify triggers.
Hydrate; reduce alcohol, caffeine, carbonated beverages.If no response, symptoms are unlikely to be FODMAP-driven; if response, tailor the long-term diet.
The course recommends starting here because it is easier and less costly; daily fiber supplement is recommended.More restrictive; use as a structured trial, not permanent blanket elimination.
🧠 FODMAP timing hook
4–6 out, 3 back: eliminate for 4–6 weeks → reintroduce one food every 3 days.
Check yourself 9
What dietary approach does the lab recommend trying before a low-FODMAP diet for many patients?
The traditional/basic IBS diet plus soluble fiber, because it is easier and less costly; move to FODMAP if there is inadequate response or the patient is motivated.
Learning Objective (LO) 1–2 · Partial genitourinary (GU) integration
The GU pieces in this block

costovertebral angle (CVA) tenderness, urinary symptoms & incontinence patterns

LECTURE pp. 9, 33–34

Stress incontinence

Leakage with increased intra-abdominal pressure without a bladder contraction. Female mechanisms listed: urethral hypermobility or intrinsic sphincter deficiency.

Urge incontinence

Sudden compelling urge immediately before/with leakage; detrusor overactivity is the female mechanism highlighted.

Overflow incontinence

Leakage/dribbling because the bladder cannot empty fully — detrusor underactivity or outlet obstruction. In men, benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is a common clinical context.

Pair the history with the exam
Dysuria/hematuria/frequency + flank pain + positive CVA tenderness pushes the differential toward upper urinary tract/kidney disease. Leakage with cough/sneeze/exertion pushes toward stress incontinence; urgency before leakage pushes toward urge; incomplete emptying/dribbling pushes toward overflow.
Check yourself 10
A patient leaks urine when coughing but has no preceding urge. Which category fits best?
Stress urinary incontinence — leakage with increased intra-abdominal pressure in the absence of a bladder contraction.
Rubric · CommunicationRubric · Parts 1–4Learning Objective (LO) 4/9 · Assessment & plan
Put the whole encounter together

Rubric-ready abdominal gastrointestinal/genitourinary (GI/GU) exam & osteopathic structural examination (OSE) selection

LECTURE pp. 4–7 · LAB rubric pp. 7–8 · transcript rubric walkthrough

Opening script — plain language

“Hi, I’m ___, a medical student working with the team. Could you tell me your name, date of birth, and what you prefer to be called?”
“I’d like to examine your abdomen. I’ll keep you covered as much as possible. Some parts may be uncomfortable; please tell me if you want me to stop at any point. Is that okay?”

Do: hand hygiene before and after, preferably where the patient sees it; re-consent before moving the drape; support comfort and positioning; explain actions in lay terms; stay professional with patient and preceptor.

Drape + position. Supine, arms at sides; expose enough to inspect and examine above and below the umbilicus while preserving modesty.
Inspect entire abdomen. Striae, lesions, scars, rashes/bruises, color, edema, distention, hernias, lipomas/masses, pulsatile aorta.
Auscultate before touching deeply. Bowel sounds in one position + aorta, both renal arteries, both iliac arteries.
Percuss six areas. 4 quadrants + epigastric + suprapubic. State tympany vs dullness.
Percuss liver and spleen. Liver midclavicular line (MCL) span; spleen with Traube/Castell-style technique.
Light palpation six areas, then deep palpation six areas. Painful area last when possible.
Palpate liver + spleen; then select symptom-driven additional maneuvers: kidney, aorta, etc.
Choose ≥3 special tests based on symptoms. Do not perform every special test indiscriminately.
Choose ≥1 OSE line based on complaint. Thoracic, rib, abdominal tissue texture changes, asymmetry, restriction of motion, and tenderness (TART), lumbar, or pelvic exam as clinically relevant.
Choose associated systems based on the differential: cardiovascular, head, eyes, ears, nose, and throat (HEENT), pulmonary, nervous, or musculoskeletal (MSK).
Symptom / complaintRubric OSE optionWhat the rubric asks
Thoracic spine complaintThoracic spineSymmetry, TART, segmental diagnosis T1–T12 with neutral/flexed/extended.
Rib complaintRibsSymmetry, TART, 1st ribs, thoracic inlet, rib motion with inhalation/exhalation, anterior/posterior bilaterally.
Abdominal complaintAbdominal regionSymmetry + TART changes; rubric notes no bony changes for the abdominal region.
Lumbar complaintLumbar spineSymmetry, TART, segmental diagnosis L1–L5 with neutral/flexed/extended.
Pelvic complaintPelvisSymmetry, TART, iliac crests, anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS), sacroiliac (SI) compression, posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS), standing flexion test.
Oral exam when indicated
For mouth pain, lymph-node changes, swallowing problems and/or nicotine use: inspect and palpate the entire oral cavity with light, gloves and gauze.
Check yourself 11
The rubric says “choose at least 3” special tests. Does that mean you should always perform the same three?
No. Choose the best tests based on the presenting symptoms and the differential diagnosis.
Learning Objective (LO) 4/9 · SynthesisLab · Cases 1–3
Think like the encounter

Case-based integration & last-pass review

LAB pp. 9–31

Case 1 · Acute lower abdominal pain

34-year-old; 4–5 h progressive 10/10 pain, movement worsens, possible fever/nausea/vomiting (N/V); T 100.8, heart rate (HR) 104, lower-quadrant tenderness + guarding.

Do not force a “cute” diagnosis. This lab case is structured to practice differential + work-up. Consider pelvic exam as appropriate, complete blood count (CBC), comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP), urinalysis (UA), and human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), and location-directed imaging.

Case 2 · Celiac

Years of episodic diarrhea, lower pain, fatigue → microcytic anemia/low ferritin → negative infection/computed tomography (CT) → positive tissue transglutaminase immunoglobulin A (tTG-IgA) + esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) biopsy.

Management pivot: gluten-free counseling + deficiency assessment + serial follow-up.

Case 3 · irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)

Years of intermittent diarrhea/constipation + bloating with unrevealing labs/imaging/endoscopy and prior IBS diagnosis.

Management pivot: validate symptoms, start basic IBS diet + soluble fiber, then structured fermentable oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides, and polyols (FODMAP) trial if needed.

Ten facts to know cold

  1. I-A-P-P exam order.
  2. Bowel sounds 5–34/min.
  3. Liver span 6–12 cm midclavicular line (MCL).
  4. Aorta width ≤3 cm on rubric.
  5. Carnett positive = abdominal wall source more likely.
  1. Rovsing/McBurney/Psoas/Obturator = appendicitis cluster.
  2. Murphy = cholecystitis pattern.
  3. Grey Turner = flank; Cullen = periumbilical ecchymosis.
  4. WRB banned in celiac: wheat, rye, barley.
  5. FODMAP: 4–6 week elimination → reintroduce one food every 3 days.
Final check
A patient with chronic diarrhea has microcytic anemia, positive tTG-IgA, and small-bowel biopsy consistent with celiac disease. Name the three grains specifically listed to avoid.
Wheat, rye, and barley.

PE Rubric 6: The Abdominal (GI/GU) System Exam Rubric with Special Tests and OSE 26-27

ABDOMINAL GI/GU · HIGH-YIELD OBJECTIVE SHEET

LO1 · Integrated GI/partial-GU history & exam

  • History (LOPQRSTA): Location, Onset, Provocation/Palliation, Quality, Radiation, Severity, Timing, Associated sx + GI/GU ROS. Ask "what lives here?" by quadrant: RUQ = liver/gallbladder; LUQ = stomach/spleen; RLQ/LLQ = bowel + reproductive/ureter; epigastric = stomach/GERD/PUD/pancreas; suprapubic = bladder/pelvic.
  • Sequence — I-A-P-P: Inspect (contour, wall movement, scars, distention, hernias, masses, visible pulsation) → Auscultate before percussing/palpating (bowel sounds + aorta/renal/iliac arteries for bruits) → Percuss (4 quadrants + epigastric + suprapubic, then liver/spleen; tympany vs. dullness) → Palpate light→deep ×6 areas, painful area last.
  • Normal anchors: bowel sounds 5–34/min (<5 hypoactive, >34 hyperactive); liver span 6–12 cm MCL, edge soft/smooth, ≤3 cm below costal margin is normal (start palpation low if hepatomegaly suspected); spleen tip palpable in ~5% normal (Traube space tympany, Castell sign for new dullness on inspiration); aorta ≤3 cm.
  • Associate abnormal → disease: bruit + pulsatile mass → AAA; involuntary guarding (persists despite relaxation) → peritoneal irritation; loss of liver dullness/enlarged span → hepatomegaly; new splenic dullness → splenomegaly; friction rub → peritoneal/organ-surface pathology.

LO2 · Specialized GI/GU tests — perform & interpret

  • Murphy: palpate RUQ under liver edge during deep inspiration → pain/inspiratory arrest = cholecystitis.
  • Rovsing: press/release LLQ → pain referred to RLQ = appendicitis (referred rebound).
  • McBurney point: focal tenderness ~2 in. from ASIS toward umbilicus = appendicitis.
  • Psoas: resisted hip flexion (or extension in lateral decubitus) → RLQ pain = appendicitis (retrocecal).
  • Obturator: flex hip 90° + internally rotate → RLQ pain = appendicitis (pelvic).
  • Rebound tenderness / heel strike: pain on release, or pain from a transmitted heel-strike jolt = peritoneal irritation.
  • Shifting dullness: central tympany/flank dullness that shifts with rolling = ascites.
  • Hernia (ventral) test: bulge appears with head/leg lift or Valsalva (↑ intra-abdominal pressure) = abdominal wall hernia.
  • CVA tenderness: fist percussion over costovertebral angle → pain = renal/upper urinary tract irritation (pyelonephritis, stone).
  • Carnett sign (bonus): tense abdominal wall, re-palpate — pain unchanged/worse → abdominal wall source; pain improves → intra-abdominal source.

LO3 · Analyze findings → assessment, differential, plan

  • Assessment = single most-likely diagnosis + the specific history/exam facts supporting it.
  • Differential = defend alternatives (VINDICATE / "what lives here"); state what supports and what argues against each.
  • Plan = tests that resolve the actual uncertainty, then treatment/disposition matched to severity — don't repeat low-value painful maneuvers in an unstable/peritoneal patient.
  • Fast pattern discrimination: burning → GERD/PUD · RUQ+Murphy → cholecystitis · epigastric→back → pancreatitis · periumbilical→RLQ → appendicitis · LLQ+fever → diverticulitis · colicky+distention+obstipation → obstruction · pain ≫ exam findings → mesenteric ischemia.
  • Work-up anchors: CBC, CMP, UA, urine hCG (if pregnancy possible); RUQ → ultrasound first; CT with IV (not oral) contrast typical for acute abdomen; mesenteric ischemia → CT angiography urgently.

LO4 · Stigmata of chronic liver disease

  • Skin/vascular: spider angiomata, palmar erythema, jaundice/scleral icterus, caput medusae (portal HTN → collateral flow opens periumbilical veins → prominent radiating abdominal-wall veins).
  • Endocrine/systemic: gynecomastia, testicular atrophy, hair loss, clubbing.
  • Other clues: parotid enlargement (esp. alcohol-related disease), Dupuytren contracture. No single finding is specific — the constellation is what matters.
  • Ominous acute-abdomen companions: Grey Turner = flank ecchymosis (retroperitoneal bleed, e.g., severe pancreatitis); Cullen = periumbilical ecchymosis; Sister Mary Joseph nodule = firm umbilical nodule from metastatic carcinoma (stomach, colon, ovary, pancreas) — an ominous finding, not chronic liver disease itself but taught alongside it.
